claim: A draft assembly of the Hi5 cell genome from Trichoplusia ni assigns 90.6% of bases to one of 28 chromosomes.
source: We report a draft assembly of the genome of Hi5 cells from the lepidopteran insect pest, Trichoplusia ni, assigning 90.6% of bases to one of 28 chromosomes and predicting 14,037 protein-coding genes.
evidence: The abstract directly states the percentage of bases assigned to chromosomes based on the genome assembly work performed.

claim: The T. ni genome predicts 14,037 protein-coding genes.
source: We report a draft assembly of the genome of Hi5 cells from the lepidopteran insect pest, Trichoplusia ni, assigning 90.6% of bases to one of 28 chromosomes and predicting 14,037 protein-coding genes.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the number of predicted protein-coding genes from the genome annotation.

claim: T. ni has undergone T. ni-specific gene expansions in chemoreception and detoxification gene families.
source: Chemoreception and detoxification gene families reveal T. ni-specific gene expansions that may explain its widespread distribution and rapid adaptation to insecticides.
evidence: The abstract states that analysis of gene families revealed T. ni-specific expansions.

claim: T. ni-specific gene expansions in chemoreception and detoxification families may explain its widespread distribution and rapid adaptation to insecticides.
source: Chemoreception and detoxification gene families reveal T. ni-specific gene expansions that may explain its widespread distribution and rapid adaptation to insecticides.
evidence: The abstract speculates on the functional significance of the observed gene expansions.

claim: T. ni has 295 microRNA-producing loci.
source: Transcriptome and small RNA data from thorax, ovary, testis, and the germline-derived Hi5 cell line show distinct expression profiles for 295 microRNA- and >393 piRNA-producing loci, as well as 39 genes encoding small RNA pathway proteins.
evidence: The abstract reports the number of miRNA loci identified from small RNA sequencing data.

claim: T. ni has more than 393 piRNA-producing loci.
source: Transcriptome and small RNA data from thorax, ovary, testis, and the germline-derived Hi5 cell line show distinct expression profiles for 295 microRNA- and >393 piRNA-producing loci, as well as 39 genes encoding small RNA pathway proteins.
evidence: The abstract reports the number of piRNA loci identified from small RNA sequencing data.

claim: T. ni has 39 genes encoding small RNA pathway proteins.
source: Transcriptome and small RNA data from thorax, ovary, testis, and the germline-derived Hi5 cell line show distinct expression profiles for 295 microRNA- and >393 piRNA-producing loci, as well as 39 genes encoding small RNA pathway proteins.
evidence: The abstract reports the number of small RNA pathway genes identified in the genome.

claim: Nearly all of the T. ni W chromosome is devoted to piRNA production.
source: Nearly all of the W chromosome is devoted to piRNA production, and T. ni siRNAs are not 2´-O-methylated.
evidence: The abstract states this finding based on small RNA mapping data.

claim: T. ni siRNAs are not 2´-O-methylated.
source: Nearly all of the W chromosome is devoted to piRNA production, and T. ni siRNAs are not 2´-O-methylated.
evidence: The abstract reports this finding based on oxidation experiments with small RNAs.

claim: Genome editing protocols have been established for Hi5 cells.
source: To enable use of Hi5 cells as a model system, we have established genome editing and single-cell cloning protocols.
evidence: The abstract states that genome editing protocols were developed.

claim: Single-cell cloning protocols have been established for Hi5 cells.
source: To enable use of Hi5 cells as a model system, we have established genome editing and single-cell cloning protocols.
evidence: The abstract states that single-cell cloning protocols were developed.

claim: Lepidoptera is one of the most species-rich orders of insects.
source: Lepidoptera (moths and butterflies), one of the most species-rich orders of insects, comprises more than 170,000 known species (Mallet, 2007; Chapman, 2009), including many agricultural pests.
evidence: The introduction cites literature to support this statement about Lepidoptera diversity.

claim: Lepidoptera comprises more than 170,000 known species.
source: Lepidoptera (moths and butterflies), one of the most species-rich orders of insects, comprises more than 170,000 known species (Mallet, 2007; Chapman, 2009), including many agricultural pests.
evidence: The introduction cites literature to support this species count.

claim: The Noctuidae family diverged over 100 million years ago from the Bombycidae.
source: One of the largest lepidopteran families, the Noctuidae diverged over 100 million years ago (mya) from the Bombycidae—best-known for the silkworm, Bombyx mori (Rainford et al., 2014).
evidence: The introduction cites literature to support this evolutionary divergence time.

claim: Trichoplusia ni is a widely distributed generalist pest that feeds on cruciferous crops.
source: The Noctuidae family member cabbage looper (Trichoplusia ni) is a widely distributed generalist pest that feeds on cruciferous crops such as broccoli, cabbage, and cauliflower (Capinera, 2001).
evidence: The introduction cites literature to support this description of T. ni as a pest.

claim: T. ni has evolved resistance to DDT.
source: T. ni has evolved resistance to the chemical insecticide Dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane (DDT; (McEwen and Hervey, 1956) and the biological insecticide Bacillus thuringiensis toxin (Janmaat and Myers, 2003), rendering pest control increasingly difficult.
evidence: The introduction cites literature documenting DDT resistance in T. ni.

claim: T. ni has evolved resistance to Bacillus thuringiensis toxin.
source: T. ni has evolved resistance to the chemical insecticide Dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane (DDT; (McEwen and Hervey, 1956) and the biological insecticide Bacillus thuringiensis toxin (Janmaat and Myers, 2003), rendering pest control increasingly difficult.
evidence: The introduction cites literature documenting Bt toxin resistance in T. ni.

claim: Hi5 cells derive from T. ni ovarian germ cells.
source: Hi5 cells derive from T. ni ovarian germ cells (Granados et al., 1986; 1994).
evidence: The introduction cites literature describing the origin of Hi5 cells.

claim: Hi5 cells are a mainstay of recombinant protein production using baculoviral vectors.
source: Hi5 cells are a mainstay of recombinant protein production using baculoviral vectors (Wickham et al., 1992) and hold promise for the commercial-scale production of recombinant adeno-associated virus for human gene therapy (Kotin, 2011; van Oers et al., 2015).
evidence: The introduction cites literature supporting the use of Hi5 cells for protein production.

claim: Hi5 cells hold promise for commercial-scale production of recombinant adeno-associated virus for human gene therapy.
source: Hi5 cells are a mainstay of recombinant protein production using baculoviral vectors (Wickham et al., 1992) and hold promise for the commercial-scale production of recombinant adeno-associated virus for human gene therapy (Kotin, 2011; van Oers et al., 2015).
evidence: The introduction cites literature supporting the potential use of Hi5 cells for AAV production.

claim: Hi5 cells produce abundant microRNAs, siRNAs, and piRNAs.
source: Hi5 cells produce abundant microRNAs (miRNAs) miRNAs, small interfering RNAs (siRNAs), and PIWI-interacting RNAs (Kawaoka et al., 2009) (piRNAs), making them one of just a few cell lines suitable for the study of all three types of animal small RNAs.
evidence: The introduction cites literature documenting small RNA production in Hi5 cells.

claim: Hi5 cells are one of just a few cell lines suitable for the study of all three types of animal small RNAs.
source: Hi5 cells produce abundant microRNAs (miRNAs) miRNAs, small interfering RNAs (siRNAs), and PIWI-interacting RNAs (Kawaoka et al., 2009) (piRNAs), making them one of just a few cell lines suitable for the study of all three types of animal small RNAs.
evidence: The introduction infers this from the presence of all three small RNA types in Hi5 cells.

claim: piRNAs protect the genome of animal reproductive cells by silencing transposons.
source: The most diverse class of small RNAs, piRNAs protect the genome of animal reproductive cells by silencing transposons (Saito et al., 2006; Vagin et al., 2006; Brennecke et al., 2007; Houwing et al., 2007; Aravin et al., 2007; Kawaoka et al., 2008).
evidence: The introduction cites multiple papers establishing the role of piRNAs in transposon silencing.

claim: The piRNA pathway has been extensively studied in Drosophila melanogaster.
source: The piRNA pathway has been extensively studied in the dipteran insect Drosophila melanogaster (fruit fly), but no piRNA-producing, cultured cell lines exist for dipteran germline cells.
evidence: The introduction states this as established knowledge about piRNA research.

claim: No piRNA-producing, cultured cell lines exist for dipteran germline cells.
source: The piRNA pathway has been extensively studied in the dipteran insect Drosophila melanogaster (fruit fly), but no piRNA-producing, cultured cell lines exist for dipteran germline cells.
evidence: The introduction states this as a gap in available research tools.

claim: T. ni Hi5 cells grow rapidly without added hemolymph.
source: T. ni Hi5 cells grow rapidly without added hemolymph (Hink, 1970), are readily transfected, and—unlike B. mori BmN4 cells (Iwanaga et al., 2014), which also express germline piRNAs—remain homogeneously undifferentiated even after prolonged culture.
evidence: The introduction cites literature supporting this characteristic of Hi5 cells.

claim: Hi5 cells are readily transfected.
source: T. ni Hi5 cells grow rapidly without added hemolymph (Hink, 1970), are readily transfected, and—unlike B. mori BmN4 cells (Iwanaga et al., 2014), which also express germline piRNAs—remain homogeneously undifferentiated even after prolonged culture.
evidence: The introduction states this as a known property of Hi5 cells.

claim: Hi5 cells remain homogeneously undifferentiated even after prolonged culture.
source: T. ni Hi5 cells grow rapidly without added hemolymph (Hink, 1970), are readily transfected, and—unlike B. mori BmN4 cells (Iwanaga et al., 2014), which also express germline piRNAs—remain homogeneously undifferentiated even after prolonged culture.
evidence: The introduction contrasts Hi5 cells with BmN4 cells, citing literature on BmN4 differentiation.

claim: B. mori BmN4 cells express germline piRNAs.
source: T. ni Hi5 cells grow rapidly without added hemolymph (Hink, 1970), are readily transfected, and—unlike B. mori BmN4 cells (Iwanaga et al., 2014), which also express germline piRNAs—remain homogeneously undifferentiated even after prolonged culture.
evidence: The introduction cites literature documenting piRNA expression in BmN4 cells.

claim: No T. ni genome sequence was available prior to this study.
source: In contrast to B. mori, no T. ni genome sequence is available, limiting the utility of Hi5 cells.
evidence: The introduction states this as motivation for the current work.

claim: Pacific Biosciences long reads and Illumina short reads were combined to sequence genomic DNA from Hi5 cells and T. ni male and female pupae.
source: We combined Pacific Biosciences long reads and Illumina short reads (Figure 1A, Table 1, and Materials and methods) to sequence genomic DNA from Hi5 cells and T. ni male and female pupae.
evidence: The Results section describes the sequencing strategy used.

claim: The initial genome assembly from long reads had 46.4 × coverage with reads >5 kb.
source: The initial genome assembly from long reads (46.4 × coverage with reads >5 kb) was polished using paired-end (172.7 × coverage) and mate-pair reads (172.0 × coverage) to generate 1976 contigs spanning 368.2 megabases (Mb).
evidence: The Results section reports the coverage statistics for the long-read assembly.

claim: The initial genome assembly was polished using paired-end reads with 172.7 × coverage.
source: The initial genome assembly from long reads (46.4 × coverage with reads >5 kb) was polished using paired-end (172.7 × coverage) and mate-pair reads (172.0 × coverage) to generate 1976 contigs spanning 368.2 megabases (Mb).
evidence: The Results section reports the coverage statistics for paired-end reads used in polishing.

claim: The initial genome assembly was polished using mate-pair reads with 172.0 × coverage.
source: The initial genome assembly from long reads (46.4 × coverage with reads >5 kb) was polished using paired-end (172.7 × coverage) and mate-pair reads (172.0 × coverage) to generate 1976 contigs spanning 368.2 megabases (Mb).
evidence: The Results section reports the coverage statistics for mate-pair reads used in polishing.

claim: The polished assembly generated 1976 contigs spanning 368.2 megabases.
source: The initial genome assembly from long reads (46.4 × coverage with reads >5 kb) was polished using paired-end (172.7 × coverage) and mate-pair reads (172.0 × coverage) to generate 1976 contigs spanning 368.2 megabases (Mb).
evidence: The Results section reports the assembly statistics after polishing.

claim: Half of genomic bases reside in contigs > 621.9 kb (N50).
source: Half of genomic bases reside in contigs > 621.9 kb (N50).
evidence: The Results section reports the contig N50 statistic.

claim: Hi-C long-range scaffolding with 186.5 × coverage produced 1031 scaffolds with N50 = 14.2 Mb.
source: Hi-C long-range scaffolding (186.5 × coverage) produced 1031 scaffolds (N50 = 14.2 Mb), with >90% of the sequences assembled into 28 major scaffolds.
evidence: The Results section reports the scaffolding statistics after Hi-C.

claim: More than 90% of the sequences were assembled into 28 major scaffolds.
source: Hi-C long-range scaffolding (186.5 × coverage) produced 1031 scaffolds (N50 = 14.2 Mb), with >90% of the sequences assembled into 28 major scaffolds.
evidence: The Results section reports the percentage of sequences in major scaffolds.

claim: Karyotyping of metaphase Hi5 cells revealed that these cells have 112 ± 5 chromosomes.
source: Karyotyping of metaphase Hi5 cells revealed that these cells have 112 ± 5 chromosomes (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The Results section reports karyotyping data shown in figures.

claim: Lepidopteran cell lines are typically tetraploid.
source: Because lepidopteran cell lines are typically tetraploid (Hink, 1972), we conclude that the ~368.2 Mb T. ni genome comprises 28 chromosomes: 26 autosomes plus W and Z sex chromosomes (see below).
evidence: The Results section cites literature to support this statement about lepidopteran cell ploidy.

claim: The T. ni genome comprises 28 chromosomes: 26 autosomes plus W and Z sex chromosomes.
source: Because lepidopteran cell lines are typically tetraploid (Hink, 1972), we conclude that the ~368.2 Mb T. ni genome comprises 28 chromosomes: 26 autosomes plus W and Z sex chromosomes (see below).
evidence: The Results section infers the chromosome composition from karyotyping and ploidy information.

claim: The T. ni genome assembly captures 97.5% of BUSCO gene orthologs.
source: The T. ni genome assembly captures 97.5% of these gene orthologs, more than either the silkworm (95.5%) or monarch butterfly (D. plexippus; 97.0%) genomes (Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: The Results section reports BUSCO completeness scores.

claim: The silkworm genome captures 95.5% of BUSCO gene orthologs.
source: The T. ni genome assembly captures 97.5% of these gene orthologs, more than either the silkworm (95.5%) or monarch butterfly (D. plexippus; 97.0%) genomes (Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: The Results section reports BUSCO completeness scores for comparison.

claim: The monarch butterfly genome captures 97.0% of BUSCO gene orthologs.
source: The T. ni genome assembly captures 97.5% of these gene orthologs, more than either the silkworm (95.5%) or monarch butterfly (D. plexippus; 97.0%) genomes (Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: The Results section reports BUSCO completeness scores for comparison.

claim: All 79 ribosomal proteins conserved between mammals and D. melanogaster have orthologs in T. ni.
source: All 79 ribosomal proteins conserved between mammals and D. melanogaster (Yoshihama et al., 2002; Marygold et al., 2007) have orthologs in T. ni, further evidence of the completeness of the genome assembly (Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: The Results section reports finding all conserved ribosomal proteins, citing literature for the reference set.

claim: T. ni has orthologs for all known D. melanogaster OXPHOS genes.
source: Finally, a search for genes in the highly conserved nuclear oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) pathway (Porcelli et al., 2007) uncovered T. ni orthologs for all known D. melanogaster OXPHOS genes (Supplementary file 1C).
evidence: The Results section reports finding all OXPHOS genes, citing literature for the reference set.

claim: The genomes of wild insect populations are typically highly heterogeneous.
source: The genomes of wild insect populations are typically highly heterogeneous, which poses a significant impediment to assembly (Keeling et al., 2013; You et al., 2013).
evidence: The Results section cites literature to support this statement about insect genome heterogeneity.

claim: The authors were unable to generate an isogenic T. ni strain by inbreeding.
source: We were unable to generate an isogenic T. ni strain by inbreeding.
evidence: The Results section states this as an experimental outcome.

claim: The T. ni sequence reflects the genome of Hi5 cells, not cabbage looper itself.
source: Therefore, our T. ni sequence reflects the genome of Hi5 cells, not cabbage looper itself.
evidence: The Results section infers this from the inability to generate isogenic animals.

claim: Hi5 cells presumably derive from a single immortalized, germline founder cell.
source: Hi5 cells presumably derive from a single immortalized, germline founder cell, which should reduce genomic variation among the cell line's four sets of chromosomes.
evidence: The Results section speculates on the origin of Hi5 cells based on their properties.

claim: Variants were called at 165,370 genomic positions (0.0449% of the genome assembly).
source: In total, we called variants at 165,370 genomic positions (0.0449% of the genome assembly), with 2710 in predicted coding regions (0.0132% of coding sequence), indicating that the genome of Hi5 cells is fairly homogenous.
evidence: The Results section reports variant calling statistics.

claim: 2710 variants were found in predicted coding regions (0.0132% of coding sequence).
source: In total, we called variants at 165,370 genomic positions (0.0449% of the genome assembly), with 2710 in predicted coding regions (0.0132% of coding sequence), indicating that the genome of Hi5 cells is fairly homogenous.
evidence: The Results section reports variant calling statistics for coding regions.

claim: The genome of Hi5 cells is fairly homogenous.
source: In total, we called variants at 165,370 genomic positions (0.0449% of the genome assembly), with 2710 in predicted coding regions (0.0132% of coding sequence), indicating that the genome of Hi5 cells is fairly homogenous.
evidence: The Results section infers homogeneity from the low variant frequency.

claim: For 88.8% of variant positions, only one copy of the chromosome has the variant allele while the other three chromosomal copies match the reference genome.
source: For the majority (88.8%) of these genomic positions (covering 0.0399% of the genome), only one copy of the chromosome has the variant allele while the other three chromosomal copies match the reference genome.
evidence: The Results section reports the distribution of variant alleles across chromosomal copies.

claim: Hi5 cells originated from a single founder cell or a homogenous population of cells.
source: We can make three conclusions. First, Hi5 cells originated from a single founder cell or a homogenous population of cells.
evidence: The Results section infers this from the variant distribution pattern.

claim: The founder cells of Hi5 were haploid.
source: Second, the founder cells were haploid.
evidence: The Results section infers this from the variant distribution pattern.

claim: Most sequence variants in Hi5 cells were acquired after the original derivation of the line from T. ni eggs.
source: Third, most sequence variants were acquired after the original derivation of the line from T. ni eggs.
evidence: The Results section infers this from the variant distribution pattern.

claim: De novo T. ni genomes assembled from male and female pupae are fragmented (scaffold N50 ≤ 2.4 kb).
source: We also assembled de novo T. ni genomes using paired-end DNA-seq data obtained from male and female pupae, but the resulting assemblies are fragmented (scaffold N50 ≤ 2.4 kb, Supplementary file 1D), likely due to the limitations of short-insert libraries and the high levels of heterozygosity commonly observed for genomes of wild insect populations (Keeling et al., 2013; You et al., 2013).
evidence: The Results section reports assembly statistics for animal genomes and cites literature on assembly challenges.

claim: The animal genome contigs are highly concordant with the Hi5 genome, with ≤1.37% of animal contigs misassembled.
source: The animal genome contigs are highly concordant with the Hi5 genome, with ≤1.37% of animal contigs misassembled (Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: The Results section reports concordance statistics between animal and Hi5 assemblies.

claim: At the contig-level, the Hi5 genome assembly is representative of the T. ni animal genome.
source: Although we cannot determine scaffold-level differences between the animal and Hi5 cells, at the contig-level the Hi5 genome assembly is representative of the T. ni animal genome.
evidence: The Results section infers this from the concordance analysis.

claim: 14,034 protein-coding genes were annotated in the T. ni genome.
source: We annotated 14,034 protein-coding genes in the T. ni genome (Supplementary file 1E), similar to other Lepidoptera (Challis et al., 2016).
evidence: The Results section reports the number of annotated genes and cites literature for comparison.

claim: The number of T. ni protein-coding genes is similar to other Lepidoptera.
source: We annotated 14,034 protein-coding genes in the T. ni genome (Supplementary file 1E), similar to other Lepidoptera (Challis et al., 2016).
evidence: The Results section compares T. ni gene count to other lepidopterans, citing literature.

claim: Orthology analysis defined 30,448 orthology groups containing orthologous proteins from two or more species.
source: Analysis of the homology of T. ni genes to genes in 20 species that span the four common insect orders (Lepidoptera, Diptera, Coleoptera, Hymenoptera), non-insect arthropods, and mammals defines 30,448 orthology groups each containing orthologous proteins from two or more species (Hirose and Manley, 1997); 9112 groups contain at least one T. ni gene.
evidence: The Results section reports orthology analysis results, citing the method used.

claim: 9112 orthology groups contain at least one T. ni gene.
source: Analysis of the homology of T. ni genes to genes in 20 species that span the four common insect orders (Lepidoptera, Diptera, Coleoptera, Hymenoptera), non-insect arthropods, and mammals defines 30,448 orthology groups each containing orthologous proteins from two or more species (Hirose and Manley, 1997); 9112 groups contain at least one T. ni gene.
evidence: The Results section reports orthology analysis results.

claim: 10,936 T. ni protein-coding genes are orthologous to at least one gene among the 20 reference species.
source: In all, 10,936 T. ni protein-coding genes are orthologous to at least one gene among the 20 reference species (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The Results section reports orthology analysis results shown in figures.

claim: T. ni contains 2,287 Lepidoptera-specific orthology groups.
source: T. ni contains 2,287 Lepidoptera-specific orthology groups (T. ni, B. mori, D. plexippus, and P. xylostella [diamondback moth]).
evidence: The Results section reports the number of lepidopteran-specific orthology groups.

claim: Far fewer orthology groups are unique to Diptera (404), Coleoptera (371), or Hymenoptera (1344) compared to Lepidoptera.
source: Far fewer orthology groups are unique to Diptera (404), Coleoptera (371), or Hymenoptera (1344), suggesting that the lepidopteran lifestyle requires more order-specific genes.
evidence: The Results section reports order-specific orthology group counts.

claim: The lepidopteran lifestyle requires more order-specific genes.
source: Far fewer orthology groups are unique to Diptera (404), Coleoptera (371), or Hymenoptera (1344), suggesting that the lepidopteran lifestyle requires more order-specific genes.
evidence: The Results section speculates on the functional significance of the higher number of lepidopteran-specific genes.

claim: The T. ni genome contains 3098 orphan protein-coding genes.
source: The T. ni genome additionally contains 3098 orphan protein-coding genes for which we could detect no orthologous sequences in the 20 reference species.
evidence: The Results section reports the number of orphan genes.

claim: 14.5% of T. ni orphan genes are present as two or more copies in the genome.
source: Of these orphan genes, 14.5% are present as two or more copies in the genome ('in-paralogs'), suggesting they evolved recently.
evidence: The Results section reports the percentage of orphan genes with in-paralogs and infers recent evolution.

claim: Some T. ni in-paralogs may have arisen by gene duplication after the divergence of T. ni and B. mori ~111 mya.
source: Some of these in-paralogs may have arisen by gene duplication after the divergence of T. ni and B. mori ~111 mya (Gaunt and Miles, 2002; Rota-Stabelli et al., 2013; Wheat and Wahlberg, 2013; Rainford et al., 2014).
evidence: The Results section speculates on the origin of in-paralogs, citing literature on divergence times.

claim: T. ni encodes ultraviolet, blue, and long-wavelength opsins.
source: The T. ni genome encodes ultraviolet, blue, and long-wavelength opsins.
evidence: The Results section reports finding these opsin genes in the genome.

claim: T. ni retains the full repertoire of insect opsins and has color vision.
source: Thus, this nocturnal insect retains the full repertoire of insect opsins and has color vision (Zimyanin et al., 2008) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The Results section infers color vision from the presence of multiple opsins, citing literature.

claim: T. ni encodes an ortholog of the non-visual Rh7 opsin.
source: T. ni also encodes an ortholog of the non-visual Rh7 opsin, which is found in a variety of insects (International Glossina Genome Initiative, 2014; Futahashi et al., 2015).
evidence: The Results section reports finding this opsin gene, citing literature on its distribution.

claim: In the D. melanogaster brain, Rh7 opsin participates in the entrainment of circadian rhythms by sensing violet light.
source: In the D. melanogaster brain, Rh7 opsin participates in the entrainment of circadian rhythms by sensing violet light (Ni et al., 2017).
evidence: The Results section cites literature on the function of Rh7 in flies.

claim: T. ni encodes an ortholog of the vertebrate-like opsin, pterosin.
source: T. ni also encodes an ortholog of the vertebrate-like opsin, pterosin, which was first detected in the honeybee (A. mellifera) brain and is found widely among insects except for Drosophilid flies (Velarde et al., 2005).
evidence: The Results section reports finding this opsin gene, citing literature on its discovery and distribution.

claim: 175 presumably Z-linked contigs (20.0 Mb) had approximately twice the coverage in male compared to female DNA (median male:female ratio = 1.92).
source: We found that 175 presumably Z-linked contigs (20.0 Mb) had approximately twice the coverage in male compared to female DNA (median male:female ratio = 1.92; Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The Results section reports coverage analysis results shown in figures.

claim: 276 contigs (11.1 Mb) had low coverage in males (median male:female ratio = 0.111), suggesting they are W-linked.
source: Another 276 contigs (11.1 Mb) had low coverage in males (median male:female ratio = 0.111), suggesting they are W-linked.
evidence: The Results section reports coverage analysis results and infers W-linkage.

claim: Sex is determined in T. ni by a ZW system in which males are homogametic (ZZ) and females are heterogametic (ZW).
source: We conclude that sex is determined in T. ni by a ZW system in which males are homogametic (ZZ) and females are heterogametic (ZW).
evidence: The Results section infers the sex determination system from coverage analysis.

claim: T. ni compensates for Z chromosome dosage in the soma: transcripts from Z-linked genes are approximately equal in male and female thoraces.
source: In the soma, T. ni compensates for Z chromosome dosage: transcripts from Z-linked genes are approximately equal in male and female thoraces (Z ≈ ZZ, Figure 2B).
evidence: The Results section reports transcript abundance analysis shown in figures.

claim: Z-linked transcripts in the male thorax are expressed at lower levels than autosomal transcripts, but not as low as half (ZZ ≈ 70% AA).
source: Z-linked transcripts in the male thorax are expressed at lower levels than autosomal transcripts, but not as low as half (ZZ ≈ 70% AA).
evidence: The Results section reports transcript abundance ratios.

claim: T. ni uses a dosage compensation mechanism that decreases transcription from each Z chromosome in the male soma, but does not fully equalize Z-linked transcript levels between the sexes (Z ≈ ZZ ≈ 70% AA).
source: These data support a dosage compensation mechanism that decreases transcription from each Z chromosome in the T. ni male soma, but does not fully equalize Z-linked transcript levels between the sexes (Z ≈ ZZ ≈ 70% AA).
evidence: The Results section infers the dosage compensation mechanism from transcript abundance data.

claim: T. ni lacks germline dosage compensation: in the ovary, Z-linked transcript abundance is half that of autosomal transcripts (Z ≈ 50% AA).
source: In contrast, T. ni lacks germline dosage compensation: in the ovary, Z-linked transcript abundance is half that of autosomal transcripts (Z ≈ 50% AA), whereas in testis, Z-linked and autosomal transcripts have equal abundance (ZZ ≈ AA).
evidence: The Results section reports transcript abundance ratios in germline tissues.

claim: In T. ni testis, Z-linked and autosomal transcripts have equal abundance (ZZ ≈ AA).
source: In contrast, T. ni lacks germline dosage compensation: in the ovary, Z-linked transcript abundance is half that of autosomal transcripts (Z ≈ 50% AA), whereas in testis, Z-linked and autosomal transcripts have equal abundance (ZZ ≈ AA).
evidence: The Results section reports transcript abundance ratios in germline tissues.

claim: T. ni compensates for Z chromosome dosage in the soma by reducing gene expression in males, but does not decrease Z-linked gene expression in germline tissues.
source: We conclude that T. ni, like B. mori (Walters and Hardcastle, 2011), Cydia pomonella (Gu et al., 2017), and Heliconius butterflies (Walters et al., 2015), compensates for Z chromosome dosage in the soma by reducing gene expression in males, but does not decrease Z-linked gene expression in germline tissues.
evidence: The Results section infers the dosage compensation pattern and cites literature on similar patterns in other lepidopterans.

claim: The T. ni W chromosome is 2.92 Mb comprising 32 contigs (contig N50 = 101 kb).
source: Our genome assembly includes the 2.92 Mb T. ni W chromosome comprising 32 contigs (contig N50 = 101 kb).
evidence: The Results section reports W chromosome assembly statistics.

claim: T. ni W-linked contigs have higher repeat content, lower gene density, and lower transcriptional activity than autosomal or Z-linked contigs.
source: In T. ni, W-linked contigs have higher repeat content, lower gene density, and lower transcriptional activity than autosomal or Z-linked contigs (Figure 2B).
evidence: The Results section reports comparative analysis of W chromosome features shown in figures.

claim: Other lepidopteran W chromosomes are enriched in repeats and depleted of genes.
source: Other lepidopteran W chromosomes are similarly enriched in repeats and depleted of genes (Abe et al., 2005; Fuková et al., 2005; Traut et al., 2007).
evidence: The Results section cites literature on W chromosome features in other lepidopterans.

claim: T. ni males produce a four-exon isoform of doublesex, while females generate a six-exon doublesex isoform.
source: T. ni males produce a four-exon isoform of dsx, while females generate a six-exon dsx isoform (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The Results section reports sex-specific splicing patterns shown in figures.

claim: The Lepidoptera-specific gene masculinizer encodes a CCCH zinc finger protein.
source: The Lepidoptera-specific gene masc encodes a CCCH zinc finger protein.

source: In the germline of D. melanogaster and other species, components of the piRNA biogenesis pathway, including Vasa, Aub, Ago3, and multiple Tudor-domain proteins, localize to a perinuclear structure called nuage (Eddy, 1975; Findley et al., 2003; Lim and Kai, 2007; Li et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2011a; Webster et al., 2015).
evidence: The Results section cites literature on nuage localization of piRNA pathway components.

source: In BmN4 cells, transiently transfected Vasa localizes to a perinuclear structure resembling nuage (Xiol et al., 2012; Patil et al., 2017).
evidence: The Results section cites literature on Vasa localization in BmN4 cells.

claim: EGFP-HA-Vasa fusion protein localizes to a perinuclear structure in Hi5 cells, consistent with Vasa localizing to nuage.
source: We used two different immunostaining strategies to detect the EGFP-HA-Vasa fusion protein: a mouse monoclonal anti-GFP antibody and a rabbit monoclonal anti-HA antibody. GFP and HA colocalized in a perinuclear structure, consistent with Vasa localizing to nuage in Hi5 cells (Figure 8C).
evidence: The Results section reports immunostaining results shown in figures and infers nuage localization.
